nameStory: This tiny lichen earned its quirky common name from its smooth, slightly glossy surface that has a remarkably similar texture to chewed gum stuck on a rock. When you run your finger over it, it feels just as smooth and slightly raised as that piece of gum someone left behind on a park bench!
description: Chewing Gum Lichen is a small, crusty lichen that forms smooth, rounded patches on rocks. It typically appears as grayish-pink to orange-pink blobs that look like they've been painted onto stone surfaces. Individual patches are usually quite small, rarely exceeding the size of a quarter, but they can merge together to form larger colonies. Despite its small size, this distinctive lichen is unmistakable once you know what to look for.

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Feels remarkably smooth and slightly waxy to the touch, just like chewed gum - this tactile quality is the lichen's most distinctive feature

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms small, rounded, blob-like patches that appear to be stuck directly onto the rock surface with no visible edges or margins

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Ranges from pale grayish-pink to bright orange-pink, often appearing more vibrant when wet and duller when completely dry

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Almost exclusively found on calcium-rich rocks like limestone, concrete, or mortar, rarely on acidic stone surfaces

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual patches typically measure 5-20mm across, though multiple patches may grow close together to form larger colonies

idTips.label: Reproductive Structures
idTips.description: Produces small, dark reddish-brown disc-like structures (apothecia) that contrast sharply with the lighter body color

habitat: Look for Chewing Gum Lichen on limestone outcrops, concrete walls, old stone foundations, and cemetery monuments throughout New England's lower elevations. It has a strong preference for calcium-rich surfaces and is often found in urban and suburban areas where concrete and mortar provide ideal growing conditions. You'll commonly spot it on bridge abutments, stone walls, and building foundations in towns and cities.

seasonality.spring: More vibrant pink-orange colors emerge as spring moisture activates the lichen, making it easier to spot against gray stone surfaces. This is an excellent time to feel the characteristic gum-like texture.
seasonality.summer: During dry periods, colors fade to pale gray-pink and the surface may appear slightly chalky, though the distinctive smooth texture remains unchanged when touched.
seasonality.fall: Fall rains restore the brighter coloration and the lichen becomes quite noticeable again. Dark reproductive structures are most commonly observed during this season.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible year-round but appears duller in color during cold, dry periods. Snow cover may obscure it temporarily, but it's still identifiable when exposed.

funFact: This lichen is so specialized for growing on calcium-rich surfaces that it can actually help you identify what type of rock or building material you're looking at - if you find Chewing Gum Lichen growing on it, you know there's limestone, concrete, or mortar present!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with small patches of actual chewed gum on concrete surfaces! The key difference is that real gum will be much softer, may have an artificial smell, and can usually be scraped off with a fingernail, while the lichen is firmly attached and has no odor.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its playful common name, this lichen is quite rare in New England, with only a single documented observation in the region. This scarcity may be due to its very specific habitat requirements or simply because it's easily overlooked due to its small size and resemblance to debris.
compareHints: Since Chewing Gum Lichen is the only Protoblastenia species documented in New England, compare it with other small pink crustose lichens in the scale lichen family. Unlike most related species, it has that distinctive gum-like smoothness and strong preference for calcium-rich substrates. Other pink rock lichens typically have rougher, more granular surfaces and may grow on a wider variety of rock types.
